english: 1) Whether the proof that $L_{+1}$ and $L_{-1}$ are $\neq 0$ is not unnecessary if instead one computes directly, by means of the theorem on the cyclotomic equation (that its left-hand side represents only primes of the form $kp+1$), $\sum^{p<N} \frac{1}{pq}$ $(q = kp+1)$, as Chebyshev and Mertens did for $\sum^{p<N} \frac{1}{q}$ ($q$ = every prime).
topic: Methodological remarks on formulas and calculation as means versus ends, followed by notes on prime number literature, the limit behaviour of a sum related to the series $\sum \ln x^n$, and a plan to rework Dirichlet's proof of infinitely many primes in arithmetic progressions.

triage.modern_statement: Fix a prime p. Hilbert asks whether the hard step in Dirichlet's proof, showing L(1,χ) ≠ 0 for the relevant characters mod p (his L_{+1}, L_{-1}, apparently the real ones), can be skipped. His proposed substitute is the elementary cyclotomic fact that every prime divisor q of Φ_p(x) = x^{p-1}+…+1 (at integer x) is either p or satisfies q ≡ 1 (mod p). From this one would directly estimate Σ_{q<N, q≡1 mod p} 1/q, in the Chebyshev–Mertens style used for Σ_{q<N} 1/q over all primes, and show that it diverges. That would give infinitely many primes q ≡ 1 (mod p) without L-function nonvanishing. The note is ambiguous as written. 'Σ 1/(pq)' may mean 'sum of 1/q over q with p | q−1'. The phrase 'dass L_{+1} und L_{-1} ≠ 0 … unnötig ist' may concern only the progression 1 mod p, or all of Dirichlet's theorem.
triage.answered_by: No single answer to Hilbert's note was found. The question was settled in the literature in two parts. (a) For the progression 1 mod n, the cyclotomic-polynomial argument is now standard. It proves infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod n) with no L-functions, and elementary expositions also treat sums of reciprocals of such primes. (b) The approach cannot replace Dirichlet's L(1,χ) ≠ 0 argument in general. Schur (1912) gave polynomial ('Euclidean') proofs for progressions a mod m with a² ≡ 1 (mod m). M. Ram Murty (1988, J. Madras Univ.; see also Murty–Thain 2006) proved the converse: polynomial-based proofs exist only when a² ≡ 1 (mod m). For the other progressions, analytic input such as L(1,χ) ≠ 0 is still needed.

evidence.claim: Cyclotomic polynomials give an elementary proof of infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod n), without L-functions. This is exactly the 'Satz der Kreisteilungsgleichung' Hilbert invokes.
The cyclotomic argument gives infinitely many primes in the progression 1 mod n, i.e. a special case of Dirichlet's theorem.

Expository account of very elementary arguments on sums of reciprocals of primes and primes in arithmetic progression, which bears on the Mertens-style estimate Hilbert wanted. Seen only through a search snippet; not checked in full.
In 1988 Murty proved the converse of Schur's result: a Euclidean proof exists for m (mod a) only if m² ≡ 1 (mod a). So Dirichlet's theorem cannot be proved this way for every progression.
Schur's and Murty's theorems characterize which progressions have Euclidean polynomials, the polynomial-based alternative to Dirichlet's analytic proof.
Murty and Thain discuss how far Euclid's elementary proof can be adapted to give Dirichlet's theorem for primes in arithmetic progressions.

triage.why: This is a real research question: can L(1,χ) ≠ 0 be bypassed in Dirichlet's theorem by using the arithmetic of cyclotomic polynomials? It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. For the progression 1 mod p, the cyclotomic route is now textbook material and does give infinitely many such primes without L-functions. If Hilbert meant only that case, the answer is essentially yes. The sources found do not show whether the reciprocal sum Σ 1/q can be pushed to a full Mertens-type asymptotic this way, and I could not check this further because I hit the search limit. If he meant replacing the L(1,χ) ≠ 0 step in Dirichlet's theorem generally, Schur (1912) and Murty (1988) show that polynomial methods only reach progressions a mod m with a² ≡ 1. That is why the answer is only partly yes, and why confidence is medium. No source links the result to Hilbert's notebook entry. Euclidean proofs of Dirichlet's theorem still appear in expository work, but this is not an active research frontier.
